title: UGC 2885
caption: The spiral galaxy UGC 2885, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGC 2885 · constellation Perseus · about 230 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and B. Holwerda (University of Louisville).

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows UGC 2885, a spiral galaxy that could be the biggest in the local universe. It lies 232 million light-years away in the northern constellation of Perseus.

Its size is hard to picture. UGC 2885 measures 2.5 times the width of our Milky Way, which is itself a large galaxy, and it holds 10 times as many stars. The word "may" matters here, since the title of largest is a possibility rather than a settled record.

A spiral galaxy is a flattened, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust, arranged in arms that wind out from a brighter center. If that title holds, UGC 2885 marks the upper end of how large a galaxy in our part of the Universe can grow.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (4.96 x 3.72 arcminutes) and distance (230 million light years), the frame spans roughly 332,000 × 249,000 light-years. Its light set out about 230 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint and distant to see without a telescope, and part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot detect.
